1.scenario: A wellness startup posts that customers who buy its $199 “neuro-optimization” subscription later report higher life satisfaction than non-buyers. The founder tells investors this proves the app *causes* well-being, citing a survey sent only to paying users (35% response) and a blogger who says psychology is “just common sense anyway.” An intern notes the company also runs a simultaneous sleep-coaching email for subscribers. A board member wants to A/B test a free vs paid group next quarter but refuses random assignment “because VIPs must get the paid tier.”

statements.text: The survey design can support a causal claim that the subscription improves life satisfaction because paying users are a naturally occurring treatment group.
statements.explain: Incorrect. The founder’s claim that the $199 “neuro-optimization” subscription *causes* higher life satisfaction rests on buyers vs non-buyers and a survey sent only to paying users—not on random assignment. Calling paying customers a “naturally occurring treatment group” still leaves self-selection (who can afford $199, who is already motivated) and the sleep-coaching emails as rival explanations, so this design cannot support that causal investor pitch.

statements.text: Nonresponse among surveyed subscribers can bias the estimated association if happier users are more likely to reply.
statements.explain: Correct. The survey went only to paying users and got a 35% response. If happier subscribers are more likely to reply, the estimated link between buying the app and life satisfaction is inflated—classic nonresponse bias that undercuts the founder’s “proof” to investors.

statements.text: Running sleep-coaching emails only for subscribers introduces a confound that rivals the app itself as an explanation for any well-being difference.
statements.explain: Correct. The intern notes sleep-coaching emails run only for subscribers at the same time as the app. Any well-being gap between buyers and non-buyers could come from that coaching, not from the $199 neuro-optimization product itself, so the founder’s causal claim is confounded.

statements.text: Refusing random assignment for VIP reasons preserves internal validity while still allowing a true experiment on causation.
statements.explain: Incorrect. The board member wants free vs paid A/B testing but refuses random assignment so VIPs keep the paid tier. That choice destroys the internal validity needed for a true experiment on whether the subscription causes well-being; VIP favoritism is selection, not a causal design.

statements.text: If psychology were only common sense, contradictory “obvious” predictions would never appear and controlled methods would be unnecessary—but history shows intuitions often conflict, which is why research designs matter.
statements.explain: Correct. The blogger’s “psychology is just common sense anyway” line is exactly the trap this statement rejects: intuitions often conflict (e.g., “buyers improved so the app works” vs “happier people buy apps”), which is why investors still need controlled designs rather than common-sense slogans.

1.scenario: A school counselor reads that “all behavior is unconscious sexual conflict” and begins interpreting every student’s lateness as Freudian resistance. Meanwhile a classmate argues psychology isn’t a science because therapists use empathy. A research methods teacher asks the class to map perspectives and to design a study of whether a new attendance app reduces lateness, with some students proposing only testimonials from friends who already like the app.

statements.text: Contemporary psychology treats Freud’s claim as a complete, testable account that replaces behavioral, cognitive, and biological perspectives for school lateness.
statements.explain: Incorrect. The counselor treats every lateness as Freudian resistance from “unconscious sexual conflict,” but contemporary psychology does not treat Freud’s claim as a complete, testable replacement for behavioral, cognitive, or biological accounts of school attendance. Mapping multiple perspectives is what the methods teacher asked for—not Freudian monopoly.

statements.text: Using empathy in therapy does not by itself remove psychology from science; scientific status hinges more on systematic observation, measurement, and testable claims in research.
statements.explain: Correct. The classmate says psychology isn’t a science because therapists use empathy. Empathy in counseling does not erase scientific status: the attendance-app question still turns on systematic observation, measurement, and testable claims—exactly what the research-methods teacher is pushing the class toward.

statements.text: Testimonials from students who already like the app are weak evidence for efficacy because of selection and expectancy biases.
statements.explain: Correct. Some students propose only testimonials from friends who already like the attendance app. Those friends are selected fans with expectancy bias, so their stories are weak evidence that the app reduces lateness for comparable students.

statements.text: A stronger test would assign comparable students to app vs no-app (or alternative support) and track lateness with predefined measures.
statements.explain: Correct. Relative to friend testimonials, assigning comparable students to app vs no-app (or another support) and tracking lateness with predefined measures is the stronger test the methods teacher is asking the class to design.

statements.text: Structuralism’s introspection method is the best modern tool for proving the attendance app causes fewer late arrivals.
statements.explain: Incorrect. Structuralism’s introspection is historically about reporting conscious elements—not a modern tool for proving an attendance app causes fewer late arrivals. Using introspection here would not establish the causal claim the class is supposed to test.

1.scenario: City hall correlates neighborhood park acreage with lower self-reported stress and announces that building parks *causes* mental health gains. Critics note richer areas have more parks, better clinics, and less crime. A consultant proposes a longitudinal study following families who move, and an aide suggests photographing smiling park users as “qualitative proof.” Another aide wants to reverse the conclusion: stress causes people to avoid parks, so acreage is irrelevant.

statements.text: The cross-sectional acreage–stress correlation alone is enough for a causal policy claim that parks reduce stress.
statements.explain: Incorrect. City hall’s acreage–stress correlation is cross-sectional and announced as “parks *cause* mental health gains.” That alone cannot ground a causal policy claim; richer areas’ clinics, crime, and wealth remain entangled with park acreage.

statements.text: Socioeconomic and healthcare differences across neighborhoods are credible third variables that can create a spurious park–stress association.
statements.explain: Correct. Critics note richer neighborhoods have more parks, better clinics, and less crime. Those socioeconomic and healthcare differences are credible third variables that can manufacture a spurious park–stress association without parks themselves reducing stress.

statements.text: A longitudinal design following movers can help by examining within-person change, though it still needs careful controls for why families move.
statements.explain: Correct. The consultant’s longitudinal plan—following families who move—can examine within-person change after park exposure changes, which is stronger than city hall’s snapshot correlation, though why families move still needs control.

statements.text: Photos of smiling visitors are sufficient experimental evidence that acreage causes population-level stress reduction.
statements.explain: Incorrect. The aide’s photos of smiling park users are not an experiment and cannot prove acreage causes population-level stress reduction. Smiles are selected, anecdotal images—not causal evidence against the critics’ confound concerns.

statements.text: Reverse causality (stress reducing park use) is conceptually possible and is one reason a simple correlation cannot settle directionality.
statements.explain: Correct. The other aide’s reverse story—stress makes people avoid parks—is conceptually possible. That directional ambiguity is why a simple acreage–stress correlation cannot settle whether parks reduce stress or stressed people use parks less.

1.scenario: A hospital IRBs a study comparing two brief anxiety workshops. Researchers plan deception about the study’s full hypothesis to reduce demand characteristics, with a planned debrief. One surgeon says deception is always unethical so the study must be canceled; a nurse says informed consent is unnecessary for staff participants; a resident wants to publish identifiable case vignettes without consent because “science needs stories.”

statements.text: IRB review and informed consent norms exist to protect participants even when the topic seems low-risk or participants are employees.
statements.explain: Correct. The hospital IRB’d two anxiety workshops, and a nurse claimed informed consent is unnecessary for staff. IRB review and consent norms still protect participants even when the topic seems low-risk or participants are employees.

statements.text: Limited deception can be ethically considered when justified, minimized, and paired with prompt debriefing—but it is not a blank check.
statements.explain: Correct. Researchers plan limited deception about the full hypothesis to reduce demand characteristics, with a planned debrief. That package can be ethically considered when justified and minimized—but it is not a blank check, which answers the surgeon’s “always cancel” absolutism without ignoring ethics.

statements.text: Because workshops teach coping, no consent or debrief is required under any research ethics framework.
statements.explain: Incorrect. Teaching coping in workshops does not erase consent or debrief duties. Canceling ethics protections because the content is “helpful” contradicts the IRB framework already in place for this study.

statements.text: Publishing identifiable clinical stories without consent violates confidentiality/privacy expectations central to research ethics.
statements.explain: Correct. The resident wants to publish identifiable case vignettes without consent “because science needs stories.” That violates confidentiality/privacy expectations central to research ethics, regardless of storytelling value.

statements.text: Demand characteristics only occur in animal research, so deception about hypotheses is irrelevant in human workshop studies.
statements.explain: Incorrect. Demand characteristics are a human-methods concern—participants guessing the hypothesis—so deception about the workshop hypothesis is relevant here. They are not limited to animal research.

1.scenario: A podcast host says Wilhelm Wundt “invented therapy couches,” that functionalists only cared about dream symbols, and that the cognitive revolution made Skinner’s reinforcement obsolete for all applied behavior problems. A student fact-checks with OpenStax-style history: Wundt’s lab introspection, James/functionalism on purpose of mind, behaviorism’s observable learning, and cognition’s return to mental processes—without erasing reinforcement science.

statements.text: Wundt is better associated with early experimental psychology laboratories and introspection than with inventing psychoanalytic couches.
statements.explain: Correct. The podcast says Wundt “invented therapy couches.” OpenStax-style history ties Wundt to early experimental labs and introspection, not psychoanalytic furniture—so the student’s fact-check of that claim is right.

statements.text: Functionalism emphasized functions of mind/behavior in adaptation more than exclusive focus on dream symbolism.
statements.explain: Correct. The host says functionalists only cared about dream symbols. Functionalism (James and related work) emphasized functions of mind/behavior in adaptation, not exclusive dream symbolism—so that podcast line fails.

statements.text: The cognitive revolution renewed scientific study of mental processes; it did not empirically abolish operant reinforcement as a useful analysis of many behaviors.
statements.explain: Correct. The host claims the cognitive revolution made Skinner’s reinforcement obsolete for all applied behavior problems. Cognition renewed study of mental processes but did not empirically abolish operant reinforcement as useful for many behaviors—matching the student’s correction.

statements.text: Skinnerian reinforcement has zero remaining relevance anywhere after cognitive psychology emerged.
statements.explain: Incorrect. Saying Skinnerian reinforcement has zero relevance after cognitive psychology emerged repeats the podcast’s overreach. Reinforcement analysis still applies to many learning and applied problems.

statements.text: Saying psychology has a single founder who also created all modern clinical methods is historically accurate.
statements.explain: Incorrect. Claiming one founder created all modern clinical methods is historically inaccurate. Wundt’s lab story does not also invent every clinical method the host mashed together.

1.scenario: An education NGO reports r = .45 between hours of tutoring and exam scores in a volunteer sample. Marketing claims each extra hour *raises* scores by a fixed amount causally. A statistician notes restriction of range (only motivated volunteers) and that tutors also provide snacks and encouragement. Someone proposes splitting volunteers by birth month as a “random” experiment.

statements.text: r = .45 shows a positive association but does not by itself prove each hour causally increments scores by a fixed amount.
statements.explain: Correct. The NGO’s r = .45 between tutoring hours and exam scores in volunteers shows a positive association. Marketing’s claim that each extra hour *causally* raises scores by a fixed amount goes beyond what that correlation alone can prove.

statements.text: Volunteer-only samples can distort estimates via selection and restricted range relative to all students.
statements.explain: Correct. The statistician flags restriction of range: only motivated volunteers. That volunteer-only sample can distort the hours–scores estimate relative to all students, so marketing should not treat r = .45 as a universal causal dose–response.

statements.text: Snacks and encouragement bundled with tutoring are potential confounds for attributing gains solely to instructional hours.
statements.explain: Correct. Tutors also give snacks and encouragement. Those extras are bundled with hours, so attributing score gains solely to instructional time ignores plausible confounds in this NGO’s setup.

statements.text: Birth-month splitting of volunteers is genuine random assignment of the tutoring manipulation.
statements.explain: Incorrect. Splitting volunteers by birth month is not random assignment of the tutoring manipulation. Birth month does not allocate who gets more tutoring hours; it cannot turn the correlational tutoring study into a true experiment.

statements.text: If r is positive, third variables are mathematically impossible.
statements.explain: Incorrect. A positive r does not make third variables mathematically impossible. Snacks, encouragement, and volunteer motivation can still drive both hours and scores in this sample.

1.scenario: A clinical team wants to know whether a new mindfulness audio reduces ICU nurse burnout. They propose: (A) a case study of one nurse’s diary, (B) a survey correlating minutes listened with burnout scores, (C) randomly assigning units to audio vs matched quiet break, measuring burnout with a validated scale. Budget allows only one primary design for a causal claim to the hospital board.

statements.text: If the board needs causal evidence about the audio’s effect, the randomized unit assignment (C) is the strongest of the three options listed.
statements.explain: Correct. The board wants a causal claim about whether mindfulness audio reduces ICU nurse burnout. Of the three proposals, randomly assigning units to audio vs matched quiet break (C) is the strongest for that causal question.

statements.text: A single diary case study (A) can vividly illustrate experience but cannot securely establish general causal efficacy for the workforce.
statements.explain: Correct. Option (A)—one nurse’s diary—can vividly illustrate burnout experience but cannot securely establish that the audio causes workforce-wide burnout reduction for the hospital board.

statements.text: The correlational survey (B) alone is equally strong as (C) for proving the audio causes burnout reduction.
statements.explain: Incorrect. Survey (B) correlating minutes listened with burnout scores is not equally strong as randomized unit assignment (C) for proving the audio causes burnout reduction; association ≠ causation for the board.

statements.text: Validated outcome measures help with construct validity regardless of design, but they do not convert a correlation into an experiment.
statements.explain: Correct. Using a validated burnout scale helps construct validity in any design, but a good scale does not turn the correlational survey into an experiment that answers the board’s causal question.

statements.text: Quiet-break controls are useless because placebo and time-off effects never threaten wellness-intervention conclusions.
statements.explain: Incorrect. Quiet-break controls matter precisely because placebo and time-off effects can mimic wellness gains. Dismissing those threats would overstate what the audio alone does for ICU nurses.

1.scenario: During a methods debate, Student A says operational definitions make concepts too “narrow” so we should never define variables. Student B says experimenter bias and placebo effects only matter in drug trials, not psychology. Student C wants double-blind procedures for a study of praise type on puzzle persistence. The TA asks which claims survive scrutiny.

statements.text: Operational definitions specify how constructs are measured or manipulated so claims can be tested and replicated—even if they feel narrow.
statements.explain: Correct. Student A rejects operational definitions as too narrow. Specifying how constructs are measured or manipulated is what lets the praise-type → puzzle-persistence study be tested and replicated—even if the definition feels narrow.

statements.text: Refusing to define variables at all protects scientific rigor better than imperfect operationalizations.
statements.explain: Incorrect. Refusing to define variables does not protect rigor better than imperfect operationalizations. Without defining praise type and persistence, Student C’s study cannot be evaluated.

statements.text: Experimenter expectancy and placebo-like expectancy effects can bias psychological studies, not only pharmacology.
statements.explain: Correct. Student B says experimenter bias and placebo effects only matter in drug trials. Expectancy effects can also bias psychology studies of praise and persistence, so Student B is wrong.

statements.text: Double-blind designs can reduce some bias when neither participant nor interacting researcher knows condition assignment.
statements.explain: Correct. Student C’s double-blind idea—neither participant nor interacting researcher knows praise condition—can reduce some bias in the praise-on-persistence study, which is why that claim survives scrutiny.

statements.text: If a study is about praise, expectancy effects are impossible because praise is not a pill.
statements.explain: Incorrect. Praise is not a pill, but expectancy can still shape puzzle persistence. Saying expectancy is impossible because the IV isn’t pharmacology repeats Student B’s error.

1.scenario: A journalist writes that a psychology lab’s failed replication means “the whole field is fake,” while quietly ignoring that the original effect was small, the new study was underpowered, and operational details differed. A scientist explains replication as a continuum and notes pre-registration and open data as reforms. The comments section claims peer review guarantees perpetual truth.

statements.text: A single failed replication can have many explanations (power, moderation, fidelity); it does not automatically license “whole field fake.”
statements.explain: Correct. The journalist treats one failed replication as “the whole field is fake,” ignoring the small original effect, underpowered new study, and changed operations. A single failed replication has many explanations; it does not license declaring the whole field fake.

statements.text: Underpowered replications can miss real effects; power matters for interpreting nulls.
statements.explain: Correct. The scientist notes the replication was underpowered. Underpowered replications can miss real effects, so a null here cannot be read as automatic proof the field is fake.

statements.text: Changed operational details can mean the replication tests a related but not identical claim.
statements.explain: Correct. Operational details differed between original and replication. That means the new study may test a related but not identical claim—another reason the journalist’s “whole field fake” leap is unjustified.

statements.text: Peer review guarantees that published findings remain true forever without further testing.
statements.explain: Incorrect. Commenters say peer review guarantees perpetual truth. Peer review does not freeze findings forever without further testing—especially when replications and reforms (pre-registration, open data) are the topic.

statements.text: Open science practices like pre-registration can reduce some questionable research practices, though they don’t magically end all error.
statements.explain: Correct. The scientist cites pre-registration and open data as reforms. Those open-science practices can reduce some questionable practices, even though they do not magically end all error—contrary to both “field fake” and “peer review = forever true.”

1.scenario: A university requires every psych major to complete a methods module after students confuse independent/dependent variables on a midterm: they labeled “hours of sleep” as DV when researchers manipulated sleep opportunity and measured reaction time. Others called a naturalistic observation of cafeteria seating an experiment because “they watched carefully.”

statements.text: In the sleep study described, sleep opportunity is the independent variable and reaction time is a dependent variable.
statements.explain: Correct. On the midterm, students labeled hours of sleep as the DV, but researchers manipulated sleep opportunity and measured reaction time. Sleep opportunity is the IV; reaction time is the DV—as this statement says.

statements.text: Careful observation alone turns naturalistic cafeteria watching into a true experiment with random assignment.
statements.explain: Incorrect. Watching cafeteria seating carefully is still naturalistic observation. Careful watching does not add random assignment or manipulation, so it is not a true experiment.

statements.text: Confusing IV/DV undermines students’ ability to interpret causal graphs and method sections.
statements.explain: Correct. Mixing up IV and DV on that sleep midterm undermines reading causal graphs and method sections—exactly why the university added the methods module.

statements.text: Naturalistic observation can be valuable for description even when it is not experimental.
statements.explain: Correct. Naturalistic cafeteria observation can still be valuable for describing seating patterns even though it is not an experiment—students were wrong to call it one, not wrong that observation can be useful.

statements.text: Dependent variables are always manipulated by the experimenter while independent variables are only measured.
statements.explain: Incorrect. This reverses the definitions students already confused: DVs are measured outcomes; IVs are manipulated (in experiments). Saying DVs are always manipulated is the same midterm error flipped.

1.scenario: A marketer claims: every smile in an ad is an operational definition of happiness; a correlational dashboard proves causation; random assignment is unethical always; placebos never affect psychology studies; peer review makes replication unnecessary. A methods instructor asks students to evaluate each slogan.

statements.text: Every smile in an ad is automatically a valid operational definition of happiness for scientific claims.
statements.explain: Incorrect. The marketer claims every smile in an ad is an operational definition of happiness. A smile on a billboard is not automatically a valid scientific measure of happiness for research claims—operational definitions must map constructs carefully, not slap labels on marketing images.

statements.text: A correlational dashboard alone proves causation of purchase by ad exposure.
statements.explain: Incorrect. The marketer’s correlational dashboard of ad exposure and purchases is said to “prove causation.” Correlation on a dashboard cannot prove that ad exposure causes purchases; third variables and selection remain.

statements.text: Random assignment is always unethical in all human research contexts, so experiments are impossible.
statements.explain: Incorrect. The marketer says random assignment is always unethical, so experiments are impossible. Human experiments with consent and IRB oversight remain possible; this absolutism would erase the methods instructor’s whole evaluation task.

statements.text: Placebo/expectancy effects never appear in psychology—only in drug trials.
statements.explain: Incorrect. The slogan that placebos never appear in psychology—only in drug trials—is false. Expectancy effects show up in psychological studies too, which is why the instructor asked students to tear these slogans down.

statements.text: Peer review removes any need for replication forever.
statements.explain: Incorrect. Claiming peer review removes any need for replication forever is the marketer’s last collapse. Peer-reviewed findings still need further testing; replication remains part of evaluating these slogans.

1.scenario: After tutoring, a methods lab correctly notes: hypotheses should be testable; IVs are manipulated when possible; DVs are measured; confounds threaten internal validity; representative sampling supports generalization.

statements.text: Testable hypotheses are central to empirical psychology.
statements.explain: Correct. After tutoring, the methods lab notes that hypotheses should be testable. That claim is central to empirical psychology and belongs in the answer key the lab is assembling.

statements.text: In experiments, independent variables are manipulated (when the design is experimental).
statements.explain: Correct. The lab correctly notes that in experiments independent variables are manipulated when the design is experimental—matching the post-tutoring checklist of what survives scrutiny.

statements.text: Dependent variables are measured as outcomes.
statements.explain: Correct. The lab treats dependent variables as measured outcomes. That is the right methods framing after they cleaned up IV/DV confusions in earlier work.

statements.text: Confounds threaten internal validity of causal claims.
statements.explain: Correct. The lab flags confounds as threats to internal validity of causal claims—exactly the kind of methods hygiene this tutoring wrap-up is meant to lock in.

statements.text: More representative sampling generally supports broader generalization (external validity concerns).
statements.explain: Correct. More representative sampling generally supports broader generalization (external validity). The lab’s note on sampling belongs with the other keepers on the post-tutoring list.

2.scenario: After a concussion clinic visit, Maya hears three takes: (1) “neurons touch and electricity jumps like wires,” (2) “her mood dip is only hormones from the pituitary painting the cortex,” (3) “sleepiness means her RAS is offline so absolute thresholds for sound became photographic.” A biopsych tutor redraws synapse, action potential, endocrine slower messaging, and sensory threshold concepts.

statements.text: Neurons typically communicate across synapses via chemical neurotransmitters rather than literal wire-to-wire touching as the clinic's first take claimed.
statements.explain: Correct. Clinic take (1) said neurons touch and electricity jumps like wires. Neurons typically communicate across synapses with chemical neurotransmitters—not literal wire-to-wire touching—so the tutor’s redraw of the synapse corrects that concussion-clinic myth for Maya.

statements.text: Endocrine signals can influence mood, but a monocausal “pituitary paints the cortex” story is too thin for a post-concussion mood dip.
statements.explain: Correct. Take (2) blamed Maya’s post-concussion mood dip on “pituitary painting the cortex.” Endocrine signals can influence mood, but that monocausal slogan is too thin for her presentation; multiple neural and situational factors remain on the table.

statements.text: Sleepiness from arousal-network disruption expands iconic sensory memory so absolute threshold becomes photographic for hours.
statements.explain: Incorrect. Take (3) tied sleepiness and RAS disruption to absolute thresholds becoming “photographic.” Sleepiness from arousal-network disruption does not expand iconic sensory memory into hours of photographic sound detection—that mash-up confuses consciousness, RAS, and sensory memory.

statements.text: Absolute threshold means she now consciously stores every photon as a permanent episodic memory of the clinic visit.
statements.explain: Incorrect. Absolute threshold is about detecting a stimulus at threshold intensity, not consciously storing every photon as a permanent episodic memory of Maya’s clinic visit. That claim invents a memory miracle the tutor’s sensory-threshold lesson does not support.

statements.text: Action potentials grow stronger without limit as they travel axons, which is why concussion recovery is guaranteed in milliseconds.
statements.explain: Incorrect. Action potentials are typically all-or-none once threshold is reached; they do not grow stronger without limit along the axon, and that myth does not guarantee Maya’s concussion recovery in milliseconds.

2.scenario: Night-shift workers drink espresso at 4 a.m., doomscroll bright phones in bed, and still feel “wired but tired.” One claims caffeine permanently stores adenosine receptors in REM only; another says bright light can’t affect circadian timing because vision is only cones for color. A colleague micro-sleeps at the wheel yet denies impairment.

statements.text: Caffeine’s alerting effects relate in part to adenosine antagonism; it does not permanently store adenosine receptors “in REM only.”
statements.explain: Correct. Night-shift workers’ 4 a.m. espresso relates partly to adenosine antagonism for alerting—not to “permanently storing adenosine receptors in REM only,” which is the false claim in the debate.

statements.text: Bright phone light at night cannot affect circadian timing because circadian photoreception only names daytime colors via cones.
statements.explain: Incorrect. Bright phone light in bed can affect circadian timing via non-image-forming photoreception pathways; saying circadian photoreception “only names daytime colors via cones” wrongly dismisses night-time light’s clock effects for these doomscrolling workers.

statements.text: If workers feel subjectively alert after espresso, micro-sleep risk while driving is scientifically impossible.
statements.explain: Incorrect. Feeling subjectively “wired” after espresso does not make micro-sleep at the wheel scientifically impossible. The colleague who micro-sleeps yet denies impairment illustrates residual sleep risk despite caffeine.

statements.text: REM rebound after deprivation means you can safely skip nightly sleep whenever espresso is available.
statements.explain: Incorrect. REM rebound after deprivation does not license skipping nightly sleep whenever espresso is available. These night-shift workers still face homeostatic and circadian sleep pressure.

statements.text: Homeostatic sleep pressure can be deleted forever by a single 4 a.m. espresso, so the two-process model is obsolete.
statements.explain: Incorrect. A single 4 a.m. espresso cannot delete homeostatic sleep pressure forever or obsolete the two-process model—“wired but tired” after caffeine is exactly why that slogan fails.

2.scenario: In a sensation lab, Ken detects a quiet tone more often when paid for hits (liberal criterion) and racks up false alarms. Lea says he “lowered his absolute threshold permanently.” Omar says Gestalt closure made the tone objectively louder. A TA introduces signal detection: d′ vs bias.

statements.text: Payoff-driven liberal criteria can raise hits and false alarms without necessarily changing sensitivity (d′).
statements.explain: Correct. Ken gets paid for hits and adopts a liberal criterion, raising hits and false alarms. Signal detection separates that bias from sensitivity (d′)—exactly the TA’s lesson versus Lea’s threshold talk.

statements.text: Lea’s claim that incentives permanently rewired absolute threshold as a sensory hardware constant mismarks a decision-criterion shift.
statements.explain: Correct. Lea says incentives permanently rewired Ken’s absolute threshold. Payoffs shifted his decision criterion (more “yes”), not a permanent sensory-hardware change—Omar’s Gestalt “louder tone” story is similarly off.

statements.text: Gestalt closure can organize perception of incomplete figures but does not literally increase the physical decibel level of the tone in the apparatus.
statements.explain: Correct. Omar claims Gestalt closure made the tone objectively louder. Closure can organize incomplete figures; it does not raise the apparatus’s physical decibel level of Ken’s quiet tone.

statements.text: Signal detection theory is irrelevant to psychology because thresholds are always fixed intensities with zero false alarms by definition.
statements.explain: Incorrect. Signal detection is highly relevant here: Ken’s pay-for-hits liberal criterion produces false alarms that a “fixed threshold with zero false alarms” story cannot explain. The TA’s d′ versus bias lesson exists precisely for this lab pattern.

statements.text: If Ken’s d′ is unchanged, calling his performance “better hearing” is misleading; he may simply be saying “yes” more.
statements.explain: Correct. If Ken’s d′ is unchanged while he says “yes” more for pay, calling his performance “better hearing” is misleading—he may only have a looser criterion.

2.scenario: A stroke survivor points toward moving lights he denies seeing (blindsight-like). A relative concludes “eyes are fine so consciousness is faking.” Another says neuromuscular junction dopamine explains conscious sight. A sensory neuroscience nurse distinguishes retina, visual cortex, and residual pathways.

statements.text: Intact eyes do not guarantee conscious visual report if cortical visual processing is damaged.
statements.explain: Correct. The stroke survivor points toward moving lights he denies seeing. Intact eyes do not guarantee conscious visual report if cortical visual processing is damaged—so the relative’s “eyes are fine so consciousness is faking” line is too crude.

statements.text: Blindsight-like dissociations show some visually guided behavior can occur without normal conscious seeing.
statements.explain: Correct. Blindsight-like dissociations show some visually guided behavior without normal conscious seeing—matching this survivor’s pointing without report, which the sensory neuroscience nurse is distinguishing from fraud.

statements.text: Dopamine at the neuromuscular junction explains conscious visual experience of lights.
statements.explain: Incorrect. Dopamine at the neuromuscular junction concerns muscle contraction, not conscious visual experience of the lights. That relative/classmate mash-up misplaces the mechanism.

statements.text: Primary visual cortex damage can disrupt conscious vision even when subcortical routes support limited responding.
statements.explain: Correct. Primary visual cortex damage can disrupt conscious vision while residual/subcortical routes support limited responding—fitting the nurse’s retina vs cortex vs residual-pathway teaching for this case.

statements.text: If someone denies seeing, all visually guided pointing must be fraudulent acting.
statements.explain: Incorrect. Denying seeing does not make all visually guided pointing fraudulent acting. Blindsight-like phenomena are the point of this vignette, not courtroom fakery.

2.scenario: At a loud concert, Priya’s pupils and heart race (sympathetic), later she feels drained. A friend says sympathetic and parasympathetic branches always fire at maximum together. Another says only the central nervous system matters for stress, so peripheral nerves are irrelevant. Someone attributes her ear ringing solely to “top-down Gestalt” ignoring intense sound exposure.

statements.text: Sympathetic activation fits fight-or-flight style arousal during the concert; later recovery often involves parasympathetic rebalancing—not perpetual dual-max firing.
statements.explain: Correct. At the loud concert Priya’s pupils and heart race—sympathetic fight-or-flight style arousal—then she feels drained. Recovery often involves parasympathetic rebalancing, not the friend’s claim that both branches always fire at maximum together.

statements.text: The peripheral nervous system carries critical traffic; saying only CNS matters for stress responding is incomplete.
statements.explain: Correct. Another friend says only the CNS matters for stress so peripheral nerves are irrelevant. The PNS carries critical traffic for Priya’s racing heart and later recovery; CNS-only is incomplete.

statements.text: Intense sound exposure is a biologically plausible contributor to tinnitus-like ringing; dismissing it as pure Gestalt top-down is risky.
statements.explain: Correct. Someone blames her ear ringing solely on “top-down Gestalt,” ignoring intense sound exposure. Loud concert sound is a biologically plausible contributor to tinnitus-like ringing; dismissing it as pure Gestalt is risky for hearing health.

statements.text: Sympathetic and parasympathetic systems are identical to the endocrine system’s glands and ducts.
statements.explain: Incorrect. Sympathetic and parasympathetic branches are autonomic divisions, not identical to endocrine glands and ducts. That conflation doesn’t explain Priya’s concert physiology.

statements.text: Bottom-up sensory intensity and top-down interpretation can jointly shape experience; extreme loudness still warrants hearing-health caution.
statements.explain: Correct. Bottom-up loudness and top-down interpretation can jointly shape Priya’s experience, but extreme concert intensity still warrants hearing-health caution—not Gestalt-only denial.

2.scenario: A dorm debates psychoactive drugs: one student calls alcohol a stimulant because it makes shy people talkative; another says opioids and caffeine share identical receptor actions; a third claims hallucinogens only affect the spinal cord. Someone sleeping off a binge is told “you can’t have REM rebound later because alcohol improves sleep architecture.”

statements.text: Alcohol is generally classed as a depressant; talkativeness can reflect loosened inhibition, not stimulant classification.
statements.explain: Correct. In the dorm debate, calling alcohol a stimulant because shy people talk more misclassifies it: alcohol is generally a depressant; talkativeness can reflect loosened inhibition, not stimulant status.

statements.text: Different drug classes act on different neurotransmitter systems; opioids and caffeine are not identical in receptor action.
statements.explain: Correct. In the dorm’s psychoactive-drug debate, one student says opioids and caffeine share identical receptor actions. Different drug classes act on different neurotransmitter systems—so that identical-receptor claim is false for this argument.

statements.text: Hallucinogens primarily alter brain synaptic signaling related to perception/cognition—not “only spinal cord.”
statements.explain: Correct. The third student claims hallucinogens only affect the spinal cord. Hallucinogens primarily alter brain synaptic signaling related to perception and cognition—not “spinal cord only.”

statements.text: Alcohol often disrupts normal sleep architecture; rebound phenomena can appear as use patterns change—so “alcohol improves architecture, no rebound” is misleading.
statements.explain: Correct. Someone sleeping off a binge is told alcohol improves sleep architecture so REM rebound can’t happen later. Alcohol often disrupts sleep architecture; rebound can appear as use changes—so that reassurance is misleading.

statements.text: Because alcohol increases social talk, it must raise dopamine at the neuromuscular junction to create vocabulary.
statements.explain: Incorrect. Social talkativeness after alcohol does not mean alcohol raises dopamine at the neuromuscular junction to “create vocabulary.” NMJ dopamine talk confuses muscle synapses with the dorm’s drug-classification debate; alcohol’s talkativeness is better framed as loosened inhibition under a depressant class.

2.scenario: An artist with monocular depth cues in a painting fools viewers into depth; a critic says binocular disparity is required for any depth perception. Separately, a patient with conductive hearing loss struggles in noise; a classmate says place theory on the basilar membrane means hearing loss must be “only psychological.” A Gestalt demo of figure-ground flips; a student claims attention cannot affect perception.

statements.text: Monocular cues can support depth perception in paintings even without binocular disparity.
statements.explain: Correct. The artist’s painting fools viewers with monocular depth cues. Depth in that painting does not require binocular disparity—so the critic who says disparity is required for any depth perception is wrong.

statements.text: Binocular disparity is important in real scenes but not the sole possible depth cue.
statements.explain: Correct. Binocular disparity matters in many real scenes but is not the sole depth cue—the painting demo shows monocular information can suffice for a depth impression.

statements.text: Conductive hearing problems are physical transmission issues—not “only psychological” because place theory exists.
statements.explain: Correct. The patient with conductive hearing loss struggles in noise; a classmate says place theory means the loss is “only psychological.” Conductive problems are physical transmission issues—not erased by the existence of place theory.

statements.text: Figure–ground organization illustrates constructive perception; attention can modulate what becomes figure.
statements.explain: Correct. The Gestalt figure–ground flip shows constructive organization; attention can modulate what becomes figure—contrary to the student who said attention cannot affect perception.

statements.text: Attention never influences perception; sensory receptors alone determine all organized experience without top-down factors.
statements.explain: Incorrect. Attention never influencing perception contradicts both the figure–ground demo and top-down factors the class is discussing; receptors alone do not exhaust organized experience.

2.scenario: During hypnosis for procedural anxiety, a patient still reports pain but less distress. A skeptic says hypnosis equals stage mind-control that deletes nociceptors. A nurse frames dissociation and focused attention; an anesthesiologist notes hypnosis isn’t a substitute for indicated anesthesia in surgery. Meditation users nearby claim they stopped needing sleep.

statements.text: Clinical hypnosis accounts often emphasize focused attention/dissociation altering experience—not literal deletion of nociceptors.
statements.explain: Correct. Under hypnosis for procedural anxiety the patient still reports pain but less distress. Clinical accounts emphasize focused attention/dissociation altering experience—not the skeptic’s “deletes nociceptors” mind-control story.

statements.text: Stage show tropes of total mind-control poorly represent ethical clinical hypnosis practice.
statements.explain: Correct. Stage tropes of total mind-control poorly represent ethical clinical hypnosis like this procedural-anxiety use—matching the nurse’s framing against the skeptic.

statements.text: Hypnosis is not an automatic replacement for medically indicated anesthesia.
statements.explain: Correct. The anesthesiologist notes hypnosis isn’t a substitute for indicated surgical anesthesia—important when someone might overread the distress reduction in this case.

statements.text: Meditation practice does not scientifically license never sleeping again.
statements.explain: Correct. Nearby meditation users claim they stopped needing sleep after seeing hypnosis reduce procedural distress. Meditation practice does not scientifically license never sleeping again.

statements.text: If distress drops under hypnosis, pain pathways and nervous system activity are proven completely offline forever.
statements.explain: Incorrect. Less distress under hypnosis does not prove pain pathways and nervous-system activity are completely offline forever—the patient still reported pain, only with altered distress.

2.scenario: A genetics article on heritability of sleep duration is misread as “genes 100% fix my insomnia, environment zero.” A twin-study student clarifies heritability is population variance, not personal destiny. Separately, a bio psych myth claims left-hemisphere people can’t feel emotion because amygdalae are only right-sided decorative tissue.

statements.text: Heritability estimates describe variance in a population/context—not a sealed personal percentage that zeroes environment.
statements.explain: Correct. Readers took heritability of sleep duration as “genes 100% fix my insomnia, environment zero.” Heritability estimates describe population variance in a context—not a sealed personal percentage that zeroes environment—as the twin-study student clarifies.

statements.text: Insomnia interventions targeting behavior/environment can still matter even when traits show heritability.
statements.explain: Correct. Even when sleep traits show heritability, behavior/environment interventions for insomnia can still matter—so the “environment zero” misreading of the article is wrong for personal care.

statements.text: Emotion involves distributed neural systems; the “left-brained people have no amygdala emotion” story is a mythic oversimplification.
statements.explain: Correct. The myth that left-hemisphere people can’t feel emotion because amygdalae are “only right-sided decorative tissue” is a crude oversimplification; emotion involves distributed systems.

statements.text: If heritability is nonzero, environmental sleep hygiene is logically impossible to help anyone.
statements.explain: Incorrect. Nonzero heritability of sleep duration does not make environmental sleep hygiene logically impossible to help. That leap repeats the article’s “genes 100%, environment zero” misreading.

statements.text: Epigenetic and experiential factors can influence how genetic predispositions are expressed in health behaviors.
statements.explain: Correct. Epigenetic and experiential factors can shape how genetic predispositions show up in sleep and health behaviors—another reason the “genes 100%, environment zero” slogan fails.

2.scenario: Lab partners argue about rods/cones after leaving a bright lecture hall into a dark theater. One insists cones alone handle all night vision; another says dark adaptation is purely psychological expectancy. A third confuses transduction with perception, claiming the retina “understands Shakespearean metaphors.”

statements.text: Rods contribute heavily to vision in low light; cones dominate bright, detailed, color vision.
statements.explain: Correct. Leaving a bright lecture hall into a dark theater, rods contribute heavily to low-light vision while cones dominate bright, detailed, color vision—so “cones alone handle all night vision” is wrong.

statements.text: Dark adaptation has substantial peripheral physiological components (photopigment recovery, etc.), not expectancy alone.
statements.explain: Correct. Dark adaptation has substantial peripheral physiological components (e.g., photopigment recovery), not “purely psychological expectancy” as one partner claimed after the light-to-dark transition.

statements.text: Transduction converts physical stimulus energy into neural signals; it is not semantic literary comprehension in the retina.
statements.explain: Correct. The partner who says the retina “understands Shakespearean metaphors” confuses transduction (physical energy → neural signals) with semantic comprehension—transduction is not literary understanding.

statements.text: Expectancy and attention can influence reports, but they don’t replace photoreceptor physiology in explaining dark adaptation curves.
statements.explain: Correct. Expectancy and attention can influence reports, but they don’t replace photoreceptor physiology in explaining dark-adaptation curves after leaving the bright hall.

statements.text: Cones exclusively mediate all scotopic night vision while rods only detect color hue.
statements.explain: Incorrect. Cones do not exclusively mediate scotopic night vision while rods only detect hue—that reverses rod/cone roles the lab partners are arguing about.

2.scenario: A viral thread insists: coffee permanently deletes the need for sleep; cones see best in pitch dark; sympathetic nerves secrete insulin as their primary job; absolute threshold means noticing every photon consciously; blindsight proves eyes are unnecessary for vision forever in everyone.

statements.text: Coffee permanently deletes the biological need for sleep.
statements.explain: Incorrect. The viral thread insists coffee permanently deletes the need for sleep. Caffeine can promote alertness temporarily; it does not erase the biological need for sleep the thread pretends to abolish.

statements.text: Cones mediate the best vision in pitch darkness compared with rods.
statements.explain: Incorrect. The thread says cones see best in pitch dark. Rods dominate scotopic vision; claiming cones win in darkness reverses the photoreceptor lesson the thread is mangling.

statements.text: Sympathetic nerves’ primary job is secreting insulin.
statements.explain: Incorrect. Saying sympathetic nerves’ primary job is secreting insulin mixes autonomic nerves with pancreatic endocrine function—another false slogan in the same viral thread.

statements.text: Absolute threshold means conscious detection of every single photon every time.
statements.explain: Incorrect. Absolute threshold is not conscious detection of every photon every time. The thread overstates threshold as perfect photon-by-photon awareness, which sensory research does not claim.

statements.text: Blindsight cases prove that literally everyone can see without eyes forever.
statements.explain: Incorrect. Blindsight cases do not prove literally everyone can see without eyes forever. The thread wildly overgeneralizes a clinical dissociation into a universal “eyes unnecessary” myth.

2.scenario: A neuro clinic correctly teaches: action potentials are all-or-none along the axon; photoreceptor rods dominate scotopic vision; circadian timing involves the SCN; selective attention filters limited capacity streams; top-down expectations can bias ambiguous percepts. A board exam asks which claims survive.

statements.text: Action potentials are typically described as all-or-none events once threshold is reached at the axon hillock/initial segment.
statements.explain: Correct. The neuro clinic teaches that action potentials are all-or-none once threshold is reached at the axon hillock/initial segment. That claim should survive the board exam.

statements.text: Rods dominate vision under scotopic (very dim) conditions relative to cones.
statements.explain: Correct. The clinic correctly teaches that rods dominate under scotopic (very dim) conditions relative to cones—keep this on the board list.

statements.text: The SCN is central to circadian timing in mammals.
statements.explain: Correct. The SCN is central to circadian timing in mammals, matching the clinic’s circadian teaching that the board exam asks you to retain.

statements.text: Selective attention reflects limited-capacity filtering of sensory streams.
statements.explain: Correct. Selective attention as limited-capacity filtering of sensory streams matches the clinic lesson and survives scrutiny.

statements.text: Top-down expectations can bias how ambiguous stimuli are perceived.
statements.explain: Correct. Top-down expectations can bias how ambiguous stimuli are perceived—another clinic claim the board exam should keep.

3.scenario: A parent stops buying candy after checkout tantrums (extinction burst follows). Simultaneously a twin’s teacher uses intermittent praise for raising hands, and an older sibling learns swear words from a YouTube “cool failure” model who gets laughs. Dad calls all three “classical conditioning of the hippocampus with flashbulb IQ.” Mom wants a functional analysis.

statements.text: Withholding candy after tantrums can put the behavior on extinction; temporary escalation (extinction burst) is possible.
statements.explain: Correct. Dad stops buying candy after checkout tantrums; behavior can go on extinction, and a temporary extinction burst (worse tantrums at first) is possible—exactly what Mom’s functional analysis should expect.

statements.text: Intermittent praise can maintain hand-raising more durably than continuous praise once behavior is established.
statements.explain: Correct. The twin’s teacher uses intermittent praise for hand-raising. Intermittent reinforcement often maintains the behavior more durably than continuous praise once it is established.

statements.text: Observational learning can transmit swear words when a model is attended to, remembered, and the behavior is motivated/reproduced—laugh tracks can function as vicarious reinforcement.
statements.explain: Correct. The older sibling picks up swear words from a YouTube “cool failure” model who gets laughs. Observational learning plus laugh tracks as vicarious reinforcement can transmit that speech—Dad’s “all classical conditioning” label misses this.

statements.text: Labeling all three as classical conditioning of the hippocampus with flashbulb IQ correctly identifies the shared mechanism.
statements.explain: Incorrect. Dad’s label—“classical conditioning of the hippocampus with flashbulb IQ”—does not correctly name shared mechanisms for tantrum extinction, intermittent praise, and modeled swearing. Those are mainly operant and observational processes.

statements.text: Classical conditioning requires a voluntary skeletal response reinforced by candy removal.
statements.explain: Incorrect. Classical conditioning is about CS–US associations, not “voluntary skeletal responses reinforced by candy removal.” Candy removal after tantrums is an operant contingency (extinction/punishment framing), which Dad mislabeled.

3.scenario: Med students cram with highlighting (fluency illusion) vs peers who self-test elaboratively. On a transfer case, self-testers win. A classmate says iconic memory lasted the whole semester so highlighting encoded permanently. Another uses availability: “I remember the bright page, so I must know sepsis criteria.” A tutor mentions desirable difficulties.

statements.text: Retrieval practice/elaboration often beats passive highlighting for transfer, despite highlighting feeling fluent.
statements.explain: Correct. On the transfer case, peers who self-test elaboratively beat highlighters. Retrieval practice/elaboration often beats passive highlighting for transfer even when highlighting feels fluent.

statements.text: Metacognitive fluency is a poor guarantee of durable, transferable knowledge.
statements.explain: Correct. Highlighting creates a fluency illusion—the page looks familiar—so metacognitive fluency is a poor guarantee that med students have durable, transferable sepsis knowledge.

statements.text: Iconic sensory memory lasting a whole semester explains highlighting’s superiority.
statements.explain: Incorrect. Iconic sensory memory lasting a whole semester does not explain highlighting’s (illusory) superiority. Iconic memory is fleeting; it cannot underwrite semester-long encoding from yellow markers.

statements.text: Availability of a bright visual memory for the page does not ensure retrieval of sepsis decision criteria.
statements.explain: Correct. Remembering the bright highlighted page via availability does not ensure retrieval of sepsis decision criteria on the transfer case—the classmate’s heuristic confuses page memory with clinical knowledge.

statements.text: If something feels hard during practice, it must be ineffective encoding by definition.
statements.explain: Incorrect. Desirable difficulties mean some hard practice (like self-testing) can be effective. Feeling hard during practice does not mean encoding failed—the tutor’s point against fluency-only study.

3.scenario: A hiring manager rejects a candidate for “not looking like a typical engineer” (representativeness) after a viral story about one bad hire (availability). HR shows base rates of successful atypical candidates. The manager says heuristics are always irrational algorithms and that IQ tests measure only phoneme awareness.

statements.text: Representativeness can lead to base-rate neglect in person judgments.
statements.explain: Correct. The hiring manager rejects a candidate for “not looking like a typical engineer”—representativeness that can neglect base rates of successful atypical candidates HR is showing.

statements.text: A vivid single story can inflate perceived likelihood via availability.
statements.explain: Correct. A viral story about one bad hire can inflate perceived risk via availability, feeding the manager’s rejection of a candidate who “doesn’t look like a typical engineer.”

statements.text: Providing relevant base rates is a rational corrective step against prototype matching alone.
statements.explain: Correct. HR’s base rates of successful atypical candidates are a rational corrective against prototype matching alone in this hiring vignette.

statements.text: Heuristics are identical to guaranteed-correct algorithms in every hiring context.
statements.explain: Incorrect. The manager says heuristics are always irrational algorithms. Heuristics are not identical to guaranteed-correct algorithms in every hiring context—nor are they always pure irrationality; the point is they can misfire here.

statements.text: Standard IQ tests are primarily phoneme-awareness batteries, so they settle engineering fit without other evidence.
statements.explain: Incorrect. Standard IQ tests are not primarily phoneme-awareness batteries and do not by themselves settle engineering fit without other evidence—another of the manager’s confusions.

3.scenario: After a smash-and-grab, witnesses watch a newscast saying the thief “crashed through glass.” Later they report glass that wasn’t there. Confidence is high. A detective trusts confidence; a psychologist cites misinformation and poor encoding under stress/dim light. A juror says flashbulb means perfect verbatim storage.

statements.text: Post-event misleading language can alter memory reports.
statements.explain: Correct. After the smash-and-grab, witnesses hear a newscast say the thief “crashed through glass,” then report glass that wasn’t there—classic post-event misinformation altering memory reports.

statements.text: Eyewitness confidence is an imperfect accuracy indicator under many conditions.
statements.explain: Correct. Witnesses’ high confidence does not make them accurate; the detective who trusts confidence alone is relying on an imperfect accuracy indicator under these conditions.

statements.text: Stress and poor viewing conditions can weaken encoding quality.
statements.explain: Correct. The psychologist cites poor encoding under stress and dim light—factors that can weaken the original memory quality before the newscast even airs.

statements.text: Flashbulb-like vividness guarantees verbatim, unchangeable memory for peripheral details like glass.
statements.explain: Incorrect. The juror’s flashbulb idea—perfect verbatim storage—does not guarantee unchangeable memory for peripheral details like glass; suggestion still produced glass reports.

statements.text: If memory were a perfect video recording, suggestion would never create glass reports—so reconstructive models fit this case better than a video model.
statements.explain: Correct. If memory were a perfect video, the newscast saying the thief “crashed through glass” could not create glass reports that were never encoded. Reconstructive models fit this smash-and-grab case better than a video-recorder model of eyewitness memory.

3.scenario: A stroke patient relearns mirror tracing across days but cannot declare the practice sessions (procedural/declarative dissociation). A PT aide says dopamine at the NMJ is “the engram.” A cognitive tutor separates skill circuits from episodic report and warns against massed one-day slideshows for emergency checklists versus spaced simulation.

statements.text: Procedural skill can improve without intact episodic verbal report.
statements.explain: Correct. The stroke patient improves at mirror tracing across days but cannot declare the practice sessions—procedural skill without intact episodic verbal report.

statements.text: Neuromuscular-junction dopamine is not a complete theory of memory engrams for mirror tracing.
statements.explain: Correct. The PT aide’s claim that dopamine at the neuromuscular junction is “the engram” for mirror tracing is not a complete memory theory. The cognitive tutor separates skill circuits from episodic report for a reason.

statements.text: Spaced, retrieval-rich simulation often beats one-day massed slideshows for durable checklist performance.
statements.explain: Correct. The tutor warns against massed one-day slideshows for emergency checklists versus spaced simulation—spaced, retrieval-rich practice often beats massed slideshows for durable performance.

statements.text: If episodic report fails, no learning of any kind is possible by definition.
statements.explain: Incorrect. Failed episodic report of the sessions does not mean no learning of any kind; mirror-tracing improvement shows procedural learning continues.

statements.text: Massed slideshows uniquely create permanent episodic flashbulb memories of procedures under stress.
statements.explain: Incorrect. Massed slideshows do not uniquely create permanent episodic flashbulb memories of procedures under stress—the opposite of the tutor’s spaced-simulation advice.

3.scenario: A language-learning app uses variable-ratio streaks. Users feel proud “insight,” then cling to wrong grammar (mental set/fixation) despite counterexamples. They call the pride proof they used perfect algorithms. A cognitive scientist distinguishes insight feelings from correctness and notes reinforcement maintaining engagement.

statements.text: Variable-ratio rewards can maintain high rates of app engagement.
statements.explain: Correct. The language app’s variable-ratio streaks can maintain high engagement rates—users keep tapping even when pride is misplaced.

statements.text: Subjective insight/pride does not guarantee the rule learned is correct.
statements.explain: Correct. Users feel proud “insight” then cling to wrong grammar. Subjective insight/pride does not guarantee the rule is correct.

statements.text: Mental set can blind learners to counterexamples that should revise a grammar rule.
statements.explain: Correct. Mental set/fixation keeps them clinging despite counterexamples that should revise the grammar rule—the cognitive scientist’s warning.

statements.text: Algorithms, by definition, never fail—so wrong grammar after “insight” is impossible if any algorithm was used.
statements.explain: Incorrect. Calling pride proof of “perfect algorithms” fails: algorithms can err, and wrong grammar after “insight” is exactly what this vignette shows.

statements.text: Affective labeling of success can coexist with operant maintenance of study behavior.
statements.explain: Correct. Affective labeling of success can coexist with operant (variable-ratio) maintenance of study behavior on the app—both pride and streaks can operate together.

3.scenario: Parents demand an IQ retest after one low group screen. The child has noisy classrooms, anxiety, and stereotype threat before timed sections. A teacher wants to cut recess to “raise crystallized g.” A counselor frames confidence intervals around scores and situational suppressors.

statements.text: A single group screening score should not be treated as immutable destiny.
statements.explain: Correct. Parents demand an IQ retest after one low group screen. A single screening score should not be treated as immutable destiny—especially with noisy classrooms, anxiety, and stereotype threat before timed sections.

statements.text: Anxiety, noise, and threat can depress timed performance without rewriting the construct of g by themselves.
statements.explain: Correct. Anxiety, noise, and threat can depress timed performance without by themselves rewriting the construct of g—the counselor’s situational-suppressor framing.

statements.text: Cutting recess is not an evidence-based method to raise crystallized intelligence.
statements.explain: Correct. The teacher wants to cut recess to “raise crystallized g.” Cutting recess is not an evidence-based method to raise crystallized intelligence for this child facing noise, anxiety, and stereotype threat.

statements.text: Crystallized intelligence lives on the basilar membrane and grows when recess is removed.
statements.explain: Incorrect. Crystallized intelligence does not live on the basilar membrane or grow when recess is removed—that slogan is anatomically and educationally nonsense in this school vignette.

statements.text: Interpreting scores requires attention to measurement error and testing conditions.
statements.explain: Correct. Interpreting the child’s scores requires measurement error and testing-condition attention—confidence intervals around scores, as the counselor frames.

3.scenario: A podcast sells “neuroplasticity gum” said to raise Sternberg practical intelligence by coating the hippocampus with crystallized g, citing self-report correlations among gum chewers. Methods students smell expectancy and non-equivalent groups.

statements.text: Self-report correlations among chewers do not validate causal practical-intelligence gains.
statements.explain: Correct. The podcast’s self-report correlations among “neuroplasticity gum” chewers do not validate causal gains in Sternberg practical intelligence.

statements.text: The biological mechanism stated is implausible as pitched.
statements.explain: Correct. Claiming the gum coats the hippocampus with crystallized g to raise practical intelligence is an implausible mechanism as pitched.

statements.text: Expectancy/placebo-like effects can inflate self-rated “street smarts.”
statements.explain: Correct. Methods students smell expectancy: placebo-like effects can inflate self-rated “street smarts” among chewers without true ability gains.

statements.text: Mentioning the hippocampus converts correlational marketing into a randomized experiment.
statements.explain: Incorrect. Mentioning the hippocampus in the gum ad does not convert self-report correlations among chewers into a randomized experiment. Non-equivalent gum-chewer groups and expectancy remain.

statements.text: Sternberg’s triarchic ideas still require serious measurement—not gum slogans—to assess practical intelligence.
statements.explain: Correct. Sternberg’s triarchic ideas still need serious measurement to assess practical intelligence—not gum slogans on a podcast.

3.scenario: Two roommates study: A rereads notes in the same order nightly (maintenance-ish / serial); B elaborates with why-questions and varies contexts. Exam asks near transfer and far transfer. A attributes B’s success to “photographic iconic storage.” B cites levels of processing and encoding specificity.

statements.text: Deeper, elaborative encoding often supports better long-term retrieval than shallow rereading.
statements.explain: Correct. Roommate B elaborates with why-questions; A only rereads in the same order. Deeper elaborative encoding often supports better long-term retrieval than shallow rereading—matching B’s exam edge on transfer.

statements.text: Varying contexts can aid transfer when tests change surface features.
statements.explain: Correct. B varies contexts; that can aid transfer when exams change surface features—near and far transfer asks in this vignette.

statements.text: Iconic memory duration does not provide semester-long photographic notes.
statements.explain: Correct. A attributes B’s success to “photographic iconic storage.” Iconic memory duration cannot provide semester-long photographic notes.

statements.text: Encoding specificity implies retrieval cues matching study conditions can help—but exclusive identical order rereading still may be shallow.
statements.explain: Correct. Encoding specificity says matching cues can help, but A’s exclusive identical-order rereading can still be shallow relative to B’s elaborative why-questions.

statements.text: Far transfer is guaranteed whenever serial order is held constant in study.
statements.explain: Incorrect. Far transfer is not guaranteed merely by holding serial study order constant—A’s strategy does not buy far transfer by itself.

3.scenario: A jury hears an expert say the defendant “matches the prototype of fraudsters” after media montages. Dim lighting and fatigue hit jurors. Defense attorney explains base rates and cognitive load. Prosecution claims heuristics equal Bayesian rationality always.

statements.text: Prototype matching can mislead relative to base-rate information.
statements.explain: Correct. The expert says the defendant “matches the prototype of fraudsters” after media montages—prototype matching that can mislead relative to base rates the defense cites.

statements.text: Fatigue and poor perceptual conditions can undermine careful systematic processing.
statements.explain: Correct. Dim lighting and juror fatigue after the media montages can undermine careful systematic processing of the fraud-prototype testimony.

statements.text: Heuristics sometimes approximate good judgments but are not always Bayesian-optimal.
statements.explain: Correct. Prosecution claims heuristics equal Bayesian rationality always—but heuristics sometimes approximate good judgments without being always Bayesian-optimal in this jury setting.

statements.text: Media montages can inflate availability of a “fraudster look.”
statements.explain: Correct. Media montages can inflate availability of a “fraudster look,” feeding the prototype judgment against the defendant.

statements.text: If a face feels typical, d′ sensitivity must have increased, making base rates irrelevant by signal-detection law.
statements.explain: Incorrect. Feeling that a face is typical does not mean d′ sensitivity increased or that base rates become irrelevant by signal-detection law—that prosecution-style leap is bogus.

3.scenario: A study-tips influencer asserts: classical CS–US pairing is identical to positive reinforcement; extinction means the animal forgets the CS forever as tissue deletion; chunking expands iconic memory to hours; misinformation only affects procedural biking skill; IQ equals the Flynn effect number for a person.

statements.text: Classical CS–US pairing is identical to positive reinforcement.
statements.explain: Incorrect. The study-tips influencer equates classical CS–US pairing with positive reinforcement. Classical conditioning pairs stimuli; positive reinforcement strengthens operant responses with consequences—they are not identical procedures.

statements.text: Extinction deletes the CS from neural tissue forever so return of responding is impossible.
statements.explain: Incorrect. The influencer says extinction deletes the CS from neural tissue forever so responding cannot return. Extinction does not permanently erase the CS; phenomena like spontaneous recovery show responding can return.

statements.text: Chunking expands iconic sensory memory duration to multi-hour storage.
statements.explain: Incorrect. Chunking does not expand iconic sensory memory to multi-hour storage. Chunking reorganizes working-memory items; iconic memory remains fleeting—another influencer mash-up.

statements.text: Misinformation effects only alter procedural memories for riding bikes.
statements.explain: Incorrect. Misinformation effects are not limited to procedural biking skill. They classically distort episodic/eyewitness reports; the influencer’s “only bikes” limit is false.

statements.text: A person’s IQ score is the Flynn effect itself.
statements.explain: Incorrect. A person’s IQ score is not “the Flynn effect itself.” The Flynn effect refers to generational rises in population scores, not an individual’s IQ number on a tip video.

3.scenario: Only one statement is worth keeping in a TA’s answer key about memory: elaborative rehearsal generally beats shallow repetition for meaning-based long-term retention. The other slogans are traps.

statements.text: Elaborative rehearsal linking to meaning typically supports better long-term retention than shallow rote repetition alone.
statements.explain: Correct. The TA’s answer key keeps elaborative rehearsal: linking material to meaning typically supports better long-term retention than shallow rote repetition alone.

statements.text: Sensory memory stores textbooks verbatim for years without consolidation.
statements.explain: Incorrect. Sensory memory does not store textbooks verbatim for years without consolidation—this slogan is a trap next to the elaborative-rehearsal key.

statements.text: Retrieval practice weakens memory every time you test yourself.
statements.explain: Incorrect. Retrieval practice does not weaken memory every time you test yourself; testing often strengthens retention—opposite of this trap slogan.

statements.text: All forgetting is only decay of iconic memory after 30 seconds in adults.
statements.explain: Incorrect. All forgetting is not merely iconic decay after 30 seconds in adults. That collapses many forgetting mechanisms into one sensory-memory myth.

statements.text: Flashbulb vividness guarantees courtroom-perfect accuracy.
statements.explain: Incorrect. Flashbulb vividness does not guarantee courtroom-perfect accuracy. Vivid feeling ≠ verified detail—another distractor beside the elaborative-rehearsal keeper.

4.scenario: A daycare advertises that Mozart flashcards cause formal operations by age four, citing kids whose parents opted in versus opt-out waitlists, plus kids parroting conservation phrases after heavy prompting. A Piagetian and a methods consultant visit.

statements.text: Opt-in enrichment groups are non-equivalent to opt-out waitlists, threatening causal claims.
statements.explain: Correct. The daycare’s Mozart-flashcard kids are opt-in enrichment vs opt-out waitlists—non-equivalent groups—so causal claims that flashcards cause formal operations by age four are threatened.

statements.text: Prompted jargon is not the same as spontaneous formal operational reasoning.
statements.explain: Correct. Kids parroting conservation phrases after heavy prompting is not the same as spontaneous formal operational reasoning a Piagetian would look for.

statements.text: Mozart packages have not been shown to yank children into formal operations as advertised.
statements.explain: Correct. Mozart packages have not been shown to yank children into formal operations as this daycare advertises—methods consultants rightly smell overclaim.

statements.text: Waitlists equal random assignment whenever parents self-select.
statements.explain: Incorrect. Opt-out waitlists with parental self-selection are not random assignment. The daycare’s opt-in Mozart group versus waitlist still leaves non-equivalent enrichment seekers.

statements.text: Object permanence failure in infants proves flashcards are the only route to hypothetico-deductive thought.
statements.explain: Incorrect. Infant object-permanence struggles do not prove flashcards are the only route to hypothetico-deductive thought—irrelevant leap from Piagetian infancy to age-four formal operations marketing.

4.scenario: Nine-month-old cries at daycare drop-off but explores with a secure base at home and calms on sensitive reunion. Relatives urge ignoring all distress (extinction) or continuous candy for silence. An attachment-informed clinician reframes.

statements.text: Separation protest can be normative; reunion quality and secure-base use are central to attachment interpretation.
statements.explain: Correct. The nine-month-old cries at daycare drop-off but explores with a secure base at home and calms on sensitive reunion—separation protest can be normative; reunion quality and secure-base use matter more than cry counts alone.

statements.text: Blanket ignoring of distress is not a sensitive shortcut to security.
statements.explain: Correct. Relatives urging blanket ignoring of all distress as “extinction” is not a sensitive shortcut to security for this infant. The child already shows secure-base exploration at home and calms on sensitive reunion—attachment-informed care fits better than ignore-all advice.

statements.text: Candy-for-silence continuous reinforcement may suppress crying without building secure working models.
statements.explain: Correct. Continuous candy for silence may suppress crying without building secure working models—the clinician’s attachment reframe against relatives’ candy plan.

statements.text: Any daycare crying proves irreversible disorganized attachment requiring candy classical conditioning of the id.
statements.explain: Incorrect. Any daycare crying does not prove irreversible disorganized attachment requiring “candy classical conditioning of the id”—a catastrophic misread of this otherwise secure-base pattern.

statements.text: Attachment patterns are relationship-and-history informed, not a one-cry diagnosis.
statements.explain: Correct. Attachment patterns are relationship-and-history informed, not a one-cry diagnosis from daycare drop-off alone. Reunion quality and secure-base use in this nine-month-old’s story matter more than treating a single protest cry as destiny.

4.scenario: A prenatal client drinks heavily and says heritability of IQ means environment is powerless. Clinic staff discuss teratogens and sensitive periods. A relative adds that twins prove parenting never matters.

statements.text: Heritability ≠ immutability; environmental teratogens can alter developmental trajectories.
statements.explain: Correct. The prenatal client says heritability of IQ means environment is powerless while drinking heavily. Heritability ≠ immutability; teratogens can alter developmental trajectories.
